title: Modern Gladiators: Body Composition Profiles of Elite Professional Fighters
content: Background/Objectives: Professional combat sport athletes represent a unique population characterized by extreme training demands, repeated high-impact loading, and strict weight-class requirements. Despite growing interest in fighter health and performance, limited data exist on comprehensive body composition and bone health characteristics among elite professional fighters across organizations and weight divisions. The purpose of this study was to assess body composition, bone mineral content (BMC), and bone min-eral density (BMD) in a cohort of world-class professional fighters and to examine sex-based differences in these variables. Methods: Fifty-two professional fighters (45 males, seven females) competing across multiple combat sport organizations (including UFC, Bel-lator/PFL, WBO Boxing, and BFKC) underwent whole-body dual-energy X-ray absorptiom-etry (DXA) assessments. Variables measured included body weight, body fat percentage, fat mass, lean mass, BMC, BMD, and bone T- and Z-scores. An independent-samples t-test was used to compare males and females, with statistical significance set at p < 0.05. Results: Of the total sample of 57 subjects, 20% (10 male, 2 female) are current or past world cham-pions. Male and female fighters were similar in age (30.1 ± 5.4 vs. 33.6 ± 5.6 years; p = 0.163). Bone health indices were notably high in both sexes, with elevated T-scores (males: 2.7 ± 1.1; females: 2.3 ± 1.1; p = 0.407) and Z-scores (males: 2.6 ± 1.0; females: 2.0 ± 1.0; p = 0.182), indicating substantially greater bone density compared to age- and sex-matched norms. Males exhibited significantly greater BMC (3728.0 ± 558.2 g vs. 2569.9 ± 344.4 g; p < 0.001) and BMD (1.5 ± 0.1 vs. 1.3 ± 0.1 g·cm⁻²; p < 0.001) than females. Body weight, lean mass, and lean mass plus BMC were also significantly higher in males (all p < 0.001). Females demonstrated a higher body fat percentage (21.0 ± 2.1% vs. 14.6 ± 2.0%; p < 0.001), though absolute fat mass did not differ significantly between sexes. Body weight (R2 = 0.427) and lean mass (R2 = 0.484) were the most significant predictors of bone mineral density. Conclusions: World-class professional fighters exhibit exceptionally high bone mineral density and favorable body composition, likely reflecting the combined effects of resistance training, impact loading, and long-term athletic development.
